utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-95-14/2-T, the Prosecutor versus Dario Kordic and Mario Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm sorry we've been delayed. What we'll do is sit for an hour and then take a break, and then sit for another hour until 12.30. Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm fully aware of the little time available to us, but I should like to say something. It won't take more than five minutes. However, I should like to raise a matter which I believe is very important for the Defence and for the trial as such, so may I have five minutes before we proceed to the examination of the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is it a matter which should be dealt with now, or can it be dealt with at the end of the day?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think this will affect the testimony we shall hear today, so the Defence should like to clarify this matter before the witness continues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Very briefly, Mr. President, Your Honours, we have now come across innovative techniques which the Prosecution has introduced in order the expedite the trial; by this I mean the summaries of witnesses' evidence which are distributed and which are then the basis for the examination of witnesses by the Prosecution. The Defence did not object to this novelty, to begin with, because the Defence should also like to see the proceedings expedited; and secondly, we did not want to oppose an experiment, an innovation, before we saw how it worked in practice. Today's witness, Mr. Munib Kajmovic, is, however, an example to which the Defence has a number of objections, and we should like to present them now. To begin with, the Defence is bound to note that this innovative method is acceptable when the Defence is given the summary at least one day, 24 hours, before the witness is examined, rather than read before the witness begins to be examined. And again, it would be quite acceptable, provided an important condition were met, and that is that the allegations in the summary as to the facts deriving from earlier statements of the witness are presented correctly and accurately, and this is something that I wish to address on this occasion. To make it easier for you to understand what I want to say, the Defence has drawn up a small table in order to show how the allegation in the summary distributed by the Prosecution simply does not agree with the facts that this allegation refers to, based on earlier statements of this witness. Will the usher please help me to distribute it?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could it also be placed on the ELMO, please, for the sake of the interpreters?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: The Prosecutor refers to earlier statements of Witness Munib Kajmovic which he allegedly made on the 13th of July '95, 27 February '97, and testimony in the Blaskic case on the 10th of January, 1998. The Defence has tried to find those statements in order to verify the allegations; however, Mr. Kajmovic has never made a statement on the 27th of February, nor did he testify in the Blaskic case on the 10th of January. The differences may not be big, but I assure you, Your Honours, that we spent a great deal of time going through the records of this case. However, what we believe is more important is on the second page of our document. In the left table there are found allegations from the Prosecutor's summary, and to the right is the statement to which a reference is made. By definition, they should be identical; however, it is not, and there are significant discrepancies. The summary says that the witness said that our client, Mr. Cerkez, was a military commander of the Vitez Brigade, and he was known as the chief commander of the HVO in Vitez; then, that nobody doubted that he was, in fact, in control of all military formations and special purpose units. Below this quotation indicated in paragraph 18 on page 3, it refers to the witness's statement of the 27th of February,'98, on page 2, in the witness's statement of the 27th of January, since there is nothing -- since the 27th February -- the statement of 27 February is non-existent, the witness said, "I know that Mario Cerkez was a commander or some commander of the HVO in Vitez and that Filip Filipovic was above Mario Cerkez." So these are two quite different, quite discrepant statements indicated in the Prosecutor's summary and in the statement of the witness. On the third page we have two more examples of this kind, in which one thing is said, reference is made to allegations, and yet in the statements and testimonies, it is completely different. If we look at number 3 in the summary which -- yes, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, we can read the examples that you gave. But these are summaries; they are no more than that. They're not evidence, and they can be no more than what the Prosecutor thinks that the witness is going to say, or dealing with those bits which the Prosecutor thinks is relevant. The evidence, of course, is what the witness gives from the witness stand, and were he to give the evidence which you say is wrongly described in the summary, then, of course, it would be open to you to cross-examine on the actual statements to show that the evidence was wrong. It can be no more than a guideline as to what the Prosecutor wants the witness to deal with, out of what may be a very considerable amount of evidence; at least, that is as I understand it. Given for the moment that these examples are right, what are you asking us to do about it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I agree with what you said, and of course I fully respect that. But with all due respect, unless we insist on the duty of the Prosecutor to present fully accurate data, then we are not saving any time because the proceedings will again then be extended, and I see then no purpose for the summaries. So yes, the Defence is for this manner of evidence, but only if these summaries are correct and that I go by the facts that are referred to. Otherwise, I really see no use of this. Moreover, the Defence believes that in a certain way, that the facts might be manipulated in this manner, and this is something that we really do not want to see. Yes, I fully know that you are all professional Judges and that you will be judging the facts in a manner in which you do that, as professionals; but nonetheless, the Defence would be much happier if these inaccurate documents were never submitted to you for your examination. So yes, we are for summaries, but only if certain control is exercised over the accuracy of the summaries, and only then, if [unintelligible] will we be able to expedite the trial. Otherwise, we shall again have the facts that we will have to argue and which will force us to conduct further investigation. That is what I wanted to say, and of course, the decision is up to you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. Mikulicic, I believe that the Chamber has already noted that this manner of examination by the Prosecution, in chief, and this manner of organising the examination, on the basis of questions which derive from previous statements, has allowed us to gain some time, and I believe the Defence has also admitted that it has allowed us to gain some time to keep better control over the hearing and to ensure a fair and expeditious trial. Now, if you are asking us that this basis -- I'm not talking about the summary; we're talking that the examination-in-chief is made on the basis of statements, and of course, yes, your request that the summaries be given you more in advance is fully legitimate. At the very beginning, we have already asked Mr. Nice -- we have told him that 24 hours in advance would be quite important, and that is quite reasonable. But as for the rest, you can intervene in different matters either at the moment when the question is asked, to correct the quotation, and that is what you said today, 27th of February. Mistakes can be found anywhere; one can find them in your documents. But you also have the cross-examination, and so far you have used it very much so that you can effectively show that there is a contradiction between the previous statement and a question or answer asked during the examination-in-chief. I believe that with all these precautions taken note of, I think we are quite satisfied now that now, owing to the cooperation between the Prosecution and the Defence on the basis of this method, we have improved the conduct of the trial, which is very important for us, as you know, and we believe that we have also managed to speed things a bit on the part of the Prosecution and on the part of the Defence. I think we can proceed in this manner, of course with all necessary improvements which may be necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, I'm sure the Prosecution have heard the criticisms which you make of this document. We have decided to proceed with these summaries, as Judge Bennouna has said, because it's a very helpful way of getting at the essence of what the witness is going to say, and it helps to concentrate the minds of the Prosecution on what they want the witness to deal with. You should clearly have the summaries in good time, and of course they should be as accurate as possible, but they are not evidence themselves and can never be. As I said, it's what the witness says in the witness stand which is evidence. With that in mind, we'll go on. Yes, Mr. Nice, would you like to call the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Incidentally, just to satisfy my friends, the statement they referred to is a statement of the -- there's a month error in the citation of the date of that statement. They had only to pick up the phone, as there's normally people here on the weekends and in the evenings, and we would have told them, as we always do if they ask us a question. Yes. Can the witness come back? Can I just add this as well while the witness is coming in? Twenty-four hours is desirable, but it's not always possible. As you know, we have a rolling programme of witnesses coming in, and our aim is to keep them here as little as possible before they give evidence. That means they are spoken to and, in the terminology of this place, proofed wherever possible the day before they give evidence. It's only when they are proofed that the documents can be prepared, and of course it's in proofing that sometimes additional material comes up. I give documents as early as I can. Indeed, I've handed to my friends this morning, in respect of the next witness, a document that's incomplete and yet to be finalised because it was only prepared yesterday. But I'll do my best. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. If you would like to take a seat, Mr. Kajmovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: For the Court and my friends, we are back at paragraph 16, having left off halfway through paragraph 22.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Kajmovic, were you present at a ceremony in Vitez in the summer of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It was a parade of HVO soldiers when they took the oath of allegiance, and we were officially invited by the HVO military structure to attend this ceremony, the oath-taking ceremony.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Where did it happen?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It happened at the town stadium in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Who spoke at the ceremony?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: There were several speakers from the military ranks who delivered particular speeches, saying nothing particular with regard to the deterioration of relations. But towards the end of the ceremony, Mr. Dario Kordic arrived, and he also delivered a speech.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tell us, please, what he said.

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Sometime towards the end of the ceremony or, rather, this review, and as far as I can remember, it was about five or six minutes before the end of it, before the end of the ceremony when Mr. Dario Kordic arrived, and he asked to be given the microphone because he wanted to address those present. He delivered the speech, and to our surprise his speech was very sharp. That is, he was delivering a message to Izetbegovic, telling him to finally notify the Muslims in Central Bosnia that this was Croat land, that they had to accept that this was Herceg-Bosna or else anything might happen. That was the gist of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When he said "anything else might happen," can you be any more particular about what he said might happen?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: What he meant was that unless a political solution was found --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: [Inaudible] the witness's conclusion from the words of Mr. Kordic, I think he should talk about facts, what he heard, but I don't think he should be permitted to express his opinions regarding conclusions that he reached from what he heard. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What did Mr. Kordic say might happen?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It is difficult for me. Now it's 1999, and that happened in 1992, and it's difficult for me to quote verbatim Mr. Dario Kordic. Naturally, I mean too much time has passed. But the gist of this whole speech was a threat to the Muslims in the Lasva Valley, that they had to accept the parastate product of Herceg-Bosna, whether they liked it or not. It was characteristic in his speech that he was addressing Alija Izetbegovic, that he should send a message to the Bosniaks in the Lasva Valley to accept that. That is, apart from addressing the Bosniaks who were sitting at home around the stadium and watching it, he was also addressing President Izetbegovic to meet his request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's far enough, Mr. Kajmovic. What you were asked is not to comment on the evidence but just tell us, if you would, what happened. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What affect did that speech have on you and, so far as you could judge it, any other Muslims who you knew had heard it?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: During that oath-taking ceremony, all people who spoke -- how shall I put it? There was certain views expressed that we did not like, but we were not particularly concerned or indignant about those speeches. But when Dario Kordic made that speech, we were all -- rather there were only a few of us present there, and we were shocked by that speech. After that speech, we were invited to the club premises next to the stadium itself and there was a cocktail party of sorts, and when we came there, Dario Kordic came to me and greeted me and said, roughly, "Well, how are you, Professor?" But we did not stay there long, but we were very shocked indeed. We could not recover after that speech. I had not had an opportunity of hearing such a harsh speech until that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 17. If necessary, can you help anybody who wants to know about the detail of damage to Muslim properties that occurred after the time you've just spoken about? Just "Yes" or "No", can you deal with damage to Muslim properties, if asked?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: That damage, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, there was considerable damage.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We've had it from elsewhere. Paragraph 18.

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, there was major damage.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: At this time between the summer or autumn of 1982 (sic) and the spring of 1983 (sic), what was Mario Cerkez's position?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: As far as I know, he was the local commander, that is, commander at the municipal level of the brigade of theirs which existed at the time. I wouldn't know any details about that, any particulars about that. I remember them better by the ultimatums they put to us, that the local troops should be placed under the command of the HVO. That is, these kind of particulars I can say something, but otherwise I couldn't tell you much about Mario Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We'll come to a particular matter of that sort a little later. But just in general, you say that he was the commander of a brigade. Does that brigade have a name or not?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think it was called the Vitez Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was there anyone in Vitez known to you to be superior to him in a military capacity?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Filip Filipovic was for a while, and then after Blaskic arrived, I believe that Blaskic was his superior.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you aware of special-purpose units in the area; "Yes" or "No"?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: We knew that there were several of those units. But their role, their task, I wouldn't know, and I'm not particularly conversant with the military organisation, but we knew there were several such units for various tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Indiscernible] or any of them?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I know that some were called Jokers, others were Vitezovi Knights, but I really don't know much about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Could you help us with the 19th of October of 1992? Was there an incident or meeting then that you recall?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Where and who was present?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: On the 18th of October, '92, I think the HVO attacked Novi Travnik, and to my knowledge, the command of our brigade, that is, the command of the army of BH in Vitez, was issued orders by Commander Hadzihasanovic to put up a roadblock in the neighbourhood community of Ahmici and another one in the neighbourhood community of Grbavica in order to prevent the passage of the HVO troops from Kiseljak and Fojnica in the direction of Novi Sad. This order was complied with, and in the evening the headquarters of the BH army in Vitez were visited by Mr. Ivica Santic, mayor, and Mario Cerkez, and they asked us -- I was present in the room. They requested that the roadblock be removed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before we move on, is this the 18th or the 19th, or can't you remember?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think it was in the night between the 19th and 20th of October, although it could also have been between the 18th and the 19th. But I think it was the 19th to the 20th.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. This was in the BH headquarters. Where were those headquarters?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. The headquarters were in the building of the secondary school in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What was said between them and you?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Since Ivica Santic came and said that he was responsible, that he was requesting the staff to remove the roadblocks in Ahmici and Grbavica, and they were told this would be done straightaway if the HVO attack against the army in Novi Travnik stopped and if they stopped sending units from Kiseljak, from Fojnica and Kiseljak. Santic then said that he could not do that, that he did not have the power, the authority, to take such a decision and that such a decision could be taken only by Dario Kordic. We then said that we could not remove those roadblocks but that we should also like to talk to Dario Kordic so as to find a solution to put an end to conflicts. Ivica Santic said to that that we could call him by telephone, if we wanted to, and that his task was only to request the removal of the roadblocks. He gave us the telephone number, and Faud Kaknjo called Novi Travnik, that is, Kordic, and got him indeed, and we were sitting around the table. At first -- Kordic did not answer the phone at first, but we could hear quite well his raised voice and invective. I think he was cursing God. He was requesting from somebody in the room in which he was to attack the Armija in Novi Travnik with all the means available until they surrendered, and then at some point he took up the telephone receiver and said no negotiations would take place until the Armija surrendered, and any proposals to that effect were simply no go. That was the end of that conversation. An hour or two after Ivica Santic and Cerkez left, a shell was fired against that room, and fortunately it hit the wall above the window, about a metre above the window, so that we escaped unscathed that night. But the headquarters had to leave that building because the HVO had attacked, and all the people had to withdraw.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: One detail. So far as the phone conversation was concerned, who from your side was going to be speaking directly into the mouthpiece of the telephone?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Faud Kaknjo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Indeed, when appropriate, who was holding the handset of the telephone?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Faud Kaknjo was holding the handset.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you nevertheless in a position to hear what you've described to the Court?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. I sat right next to him, and we were listening very carefully. We sort of leaned in towards Faud Kaknjo so we would be able to follow the conversation, and I was able to here it. I believe some other people were also able to hear it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The second part of paragraph 22. Between the latter half of 1992 and the spring of 1993, were there any moderate Croats, or Croats who you judged to be moderate, who found themselves in positions of leadership or holding office, and if so, what happened to them?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: One could give some examples where some more moderate people were involved, but at the top positions on the local level, you could not say that there were any moderates. Perhaps at lower levels, there were some, but I believe that even if such people existed, I think that they were not able to manifest that because they were afraid of being sanctioned by the leadership of the HVO. Perhaps Ivan Budimir would be an example of that kind, and later on he was killed by them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you see Dario Kordic at any time between the oath-taking ceremony in the summer and the spring of '93, and if so, how was he dressed and how was he addressed?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did not see him, for the most part, except I saw him on television several times, and the television was broadcasting press conferences out of Busovaca. He wore a uniform and he was addressed as "Colonel". That is the rank that he had been accorded then. And also he often had a rosary with a cross which he held.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 23 we've I think substantially dealt with. 24, towards the end of 1992, or thereabouts, were you aware of soldiers present in Vitez who were not local to Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tell us about them, in just a sentence or so.

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: This was a group of soldiers, perhaps about ten men, who were billeted in a house across the street from my own. They were Ivo Pocanja had a coffee bar called Patria, and that's where they were staying. Sometimes they would leave this house in uniforms, sometimes in civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And what could you tell about their origins? Where did they come from?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did not know these men because I had never seen them before in the territory of the municipality. One day I was passing by that house, and one of them stopped me and asked to exchange some money. He was looking to exchange some money, to exchange it into foreign currency. From his accent, I could see that they were people either from eastern Herzegovina or from Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can I now deal with an incident in January 1993 involving Mario Cerkez. Was there an incident there that you can recall and tell us about, please?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. On several occasions the HVO and HDZ structures -- that is, the local HVO government -- sent us ultimatums; in other words, they demanded that the BH army be placed under the control of the HVO. Among these people was also Mario Cerkez. So those were the only contacts which I had with Mario Cerkez. On several occasions they asked that we accept their command, and of course they gave us ultimatums; at first not openly, but later on they were open. I believe that one such ultimatum was given in January 1993, when Mario Cerkez expressly told us that if we did not accept this command by noon the next day, that shelling would start; that is, that the HVO would carry out an attack. Of course, we could not accept this, because this would mean a direct attack on the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina. It was counter to all the laws of the country.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you break your narrative to tell us this: Was it explained where the shelling would take place?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: These ultimatums did not specify what locations would be attacked, but we were told that if we did not accept it -- in other words, one of the ultimatums was, if you don't accept this by 12.00 noon tomorrow, we would start an attack. So these were the forms of pressure that they employed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You didn't accept this ultimatum. In the event, was there any shelling?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, there was no shelling. Specifically on that ultimatum, we had even accepted it, because militarily we were not organised enough in order to counter the HVO, and with respect to one of these ultimatums, formally we took a position to accept it. But on that day, when 12.00 noon came, Mario Cerkez did not make a phone call, and the situation just remained tense, and they did not do anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: At that stage, what part of Vitez were you living in?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I lived in the new part of Vitez, but we held our meetings in the old part of Vitez. That is where the headquarters were after we had been driven out of the school centre, the secondary school centre, in October '92.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And the old part of Vitez, Stari Vitez, what was the majority population there?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The majority was the Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What approximate percentage occupation, by one ethnic group and another, was there in Stari Vitez leading up to the spring of 1993?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: There were about 1.200 to 1.400 inhabitants in Stari Vitez. Out of them, 200, 250 were Croats, and the rest were Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 15th of April, 1993, please: Did you meet Mario Cerkez?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Briefly, at the fire station in Stari Vitez. A ceremony was held there that was to celebrate BH Army Day. That day is taken as the day of establishment of the BH army. Mario Cerkez came to this ceremony. He did not stay long because an incident had taken place -- I don't know the details, but there was a gas station, and he and some members of the BH army went there to try to solve the problem, so that I saw him that day in the fire station in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What passed between you?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: He had been invited to this ceremony. We sat around the table, and meanwhile, as I said, this incident took place, so that essentially nothing important happened in the fire station that day, except that they were negotiating with the military structures to normalise the relations, and that the next day -- that is, on 16 April -- a match should take place between the BH army and the HVO members.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What sort of a match?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: A soccer match.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. What time of the day, if you can recall, was this encounter, this meeting with Cerkez?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: As far as I recall, this was sometime in the afternoon. Perhaps 3.00 in the afternoon; sometime around that time, even though I am not sure. But it was on that day, because on that day there was the ceremony which he attended briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On the 15th of April -- just "Yes" or "No" to this -- was there a press conference by Kordic of which you subsequently became aware? Just "Yes" or "No."

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How soon after the press conference apparently occurred did you learn of it? Same day, subsequent day?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I learned of it as early as that evening, around 9.00, 9.00 p.m., from people with whom I had contact, because I was asked whether I had seen this press conference and what I thought about it. Then, of course, later on, during the military conflict, this conference was discussed at quite some length.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What was your understanding of what was said in the conference?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I have to object on the grounds of unreliable hearsay at -- who knows how many hands, Your Honour? This witness didn't see the press conference, so all he is trying to do is to relate what other people, who may or my not have seen the press conference, heard about it and concluded from it. I think, under Rule 89(B) and (C), that sort of evidence is unduly prejudicial and has virtually no probative value and therefore should be excluded. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, perhaps you can establish at what hand he heard about the conference.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: First of all, was it one person or more than one person who told you about the conference?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Regarding this conference, personally, to date, to date, among us who were in some positions there, we are still --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It will help, Mr. Kajmovic, if you just answer the quite specific questions I ask, at least at the moment. On the day itself, was it from one person or more than one person that you heard about the conference?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: From several persons, and they all believed that this was a speech that was going to --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you again. Did you understand that one of those people or more than one of those people had heard the conference on the television or radio themselves?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, several people.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you give an idea of how many people speaking to you had apparently heard the conference themselves? One, two, however many.

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Several. Several people. I don't know the number, but several people told me about it. Not right away, but over a longer period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But I'm just concerned now with the same day. On that day, when you learnt about it, whoever told you about it, how long before they told you about it had it apparently happened? In terms of minutes, hours, or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I heard about it sometime around 9.00 p.m. on 15 April, '93.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And apparently it had happened at what time in the day itself?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The conference was sometime in the afternoon on 15 April, in Busovaca; but as far as I heard, this conference was broadcast twice on local television. I think it was once around 5.00 p.m. and again around 7.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were the accounts that you heard, from people who had apparently seen or heard the conference, were they consistent one with another, or were they at odds one with another?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: They related approximately the same thing, that this was a declaration of war and that there will be an attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's all I asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Very briefly, Your Honour, we have no objection to any videotape of this alleged TV conference or any transcript of the alleged radio programme. Apparently it was broadcast several times. If there's such a transcript, then obviously that's the best evidence of what was said. But this sort of anecdotal information, derived from an variety of unidentified people over an apparently substantial period of time, is absolutely the essence of something that is untrustworthy and unreliable, and for that reason we object to it. Thank you. (Trial Chamber confers)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We shall admit this evidence. The reports which the witness heard were heard on the very same day as the conference was given, and therefore, to that extent, are likely to be more reliable.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tell us, please, what you were told, by those who heard the press conference, of its content.

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: If I can only just make one comment, please: Kordic's speech on 15 April was confirmed in 5.30 a.m. on 16 April, and everybody --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, look, Mr. Kajmovic, we will all get on more quickly if you would just answer the questions. What was it that you heard was said at the press conference? Could you please concentrate on that.

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did not hear the speech given at the press conference, but people warned me, they levelled criticism against me: Why did we not prepare against the HVO attack when it was clear that it was going to happen following Kordic's speech?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, we are not going to get on --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's problems with -- perhaps cultures. Can I try once more?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Kajmovic, it will help, I'm sure, if you listen to the questions and just answer the question. Now, what were you told as to the content of the press conference? That is to say, what were you told Kordic had said in the press conference? That's all we want to hear.

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It said that war was practically inevitable, and so everybody was in fear of what was going to happen that night. They did not say -- I was not told that Kordic had openly and directly said that this was going to take place, but everybody concluded from this speech that this is what was going to follow -- whether the next day or two days, but soon.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let me stop you again. From what you were told, which you say was broadly consistent one account with other, can you help the Judges at all with the words or the things that Kordic was said, by those people listening to the broadcast, to have said? If you can't help us with any particular words or any particular things that he said, we'll move on; but if you can help, then please do so.

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I do not recall these details, but people called us and criticised us because we were people who were supposed to produce these judgements --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I understand that. If you can't recall the words, I'm going to move on. We may come back to that topic later, but not for the time being. The first you knew of any attack by any party was at what time and on what day?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: You mean when the attack took place?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I was asleep in Stari Vitez, and about 4.30 I was awakened by the shells which were falling on Stari Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm now going to deal with the attack on Stari Vitez in absolute summary, and I don't want you to trouble yourself with detail, because it's been dealt with by other witnesses and may be dealt with by other witnesses to come, so we don't need to deal with things repeatedly, but just answer these questions with one or two words, if that's appropriate. How long did the attack on Stari Vitez last?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The attack started on 16 April, around 5.30, about half past 5.00, and it basically ended 25 February, 1994, when the cease-fire took effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Within that long period of time, were there major offensives as opposed to continuing lesser offensives?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Included in those mayor incidents, was there the truck-bomb attack?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, this took place on the third day of the attack; that is, on 18 April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was there a further attack in July?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: For the assistance of my friends, the statement of the 27th of February, page 3 -- January, page 3.

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, there was major attack on 18 July '93; there was another one in late January '94.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. Nice, there's an error in the date, on the transcript. Maybe it comes from the witness. He mentioned the 25th of February, that the attack started on 16 April, half past 5.00, and it basically ended -- that means -- no, perhaps it's not a mistake. It means the attack ended on 25th February, 1994, the year after?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Exactly, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The one detail only from the 18th of July '93 attack -- and again, single-word answers will help the Court most -- at that time, was Stari Vitez being defended by yourself and others or by various people on the Muslim side? Just "Yes" or "No."

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, Bosnian side, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In the course of that attack, did the Bosniak side lose any soldiers, or none?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: There were no killed, just some wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did the HVO lose soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were some of their soldiers left lying in territory that was under Muslim control?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were the bodies of those soldiers searched?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, with the assistance of UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And was paper found on one body, one soldier in particular, identifying where he had come from?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I received such information from the headquarters, that among the killed soldiers was a Croat soldier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Sayers, now, what is the point here?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I just would like a point of clarification, Your Honour, as to whether this is his personal knowledge or whether he is reciting something that he learned from other people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No doubt that can be established.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think you've told us -- the information about the identification of the soldier came from where?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I received it from a staff member, the army staff members, Nenad. It was their information, and based on his personal identification papers, they saw that he had come from Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Pausing there, the man Nenad, to your knowledge, had he been the person to see the identification papers himself, or not, or don't you know?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I'm not sure that I know what document you're referring to. Are you referring to the personal ID documents? I don't know what the soldier's name was, but Nihad Rebikic is the name of the BH army staff, and he told me that he saw the documents of this killed soldier and that he was from Croatia. I don't know whether his name was Nenad or something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Forget Nenad; it was my mistake. I see the time. I recall what the Chamber said about the break it was going to take, but I'm entirely in your hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: How much longer are you going to be?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: By the time I deal with it and an objection that I know is coming up, another ten minutes, I should think, at least.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll take the break now. A quarter of an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: To complete the history of Stari Vitez and the attacks on it, you've made reference to a third major attack. When was that?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The first major attack was the beginning, that is, the 16th of April. The second --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm going to cut you short. Please listen to the questions. The Chamber already knows about the first and the second attack. When was the third attack?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The third attack took place on the 22nd, in the evening, the 23rd, in the evening, and the 24th, in the evening. The 22nd, the 23rd, and the 24th of February, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The nature of this attack, was it an attack by shells?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: These were attacks that went on throughout the night with shells and an attempt at an infantry attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would object to this question. I think that this question is clearly out of the time which is indicted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I can't see that it does any harm at all. Go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I've asked all I wanted to ask about it, save only for this:

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In the course of the overall fighting or attacks at and on Stari Vitez or from it, were any people from Stari Vitez taken prisoner by the HVO or not?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: During the attack, if you mean during the attack --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, not then.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were soldiers killed in the course of the attack; "Yes" or "No"?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: On the side of the BH army, there were wounded, and possibly some people may have been killed, but I don't know the details. As for the HVO side, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 30, and I hope that my friends won't object if I put to the witness, to save time, the appointments he had. Just please listen to this,

utterances.speaker: MR. KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: Did you spend the entire time of this conflict in Stari Vitez, apart, I think, from a couple of occasions when you left with UNPROFOR or some other assistance?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you appointed commander of the civilian police, were you in charge of food distribution and burial of the dead?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. I was commander of the civil defence staff, not the police, whose task it was to distribute food, some of the food we had in reserve, and to bury the dead and killed. That was the primary role and task of the civil defence staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Following the conflict in -- at the end of the conflict in February, 1994, did you go to live in Zenica, where you are still working, you being unable to return to Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. Three months later, I left Stari Vitez. I am living in Zenica to this day.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Two other paragraphs I want to return to, one as I promised last week. But first paragraph 28. I want you, please, to answer these questions strictly "Yes" or "No" or by single words where that is possible. Did you learn of Kordic's whereabouts on the day of the 16th of April; "Yes" or "No"?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Once again, Your Honour, I object to this, and I'm specifically referring to page 6 of the first statement that Mr. Kajmovic gave on the 13th of July, 1995. The basis of this information is quite explicitly a rumour, and that's the word that's used in this statement, and that kind of testimony should not be admissible for the same reasons I have previously articulated under Rule 89(B) and C. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, perhaps you can establish, with some care, the basis of this evidence, and particularly if it's as a result of a rumour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So, first of all, just "Yes" or "No". Did you discover his whereabouts or, to be precise, his apparent whereabouts, just "Yes" or "No"?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did receive information that it was in the post office in Vitez --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Stop there, please. Please, will you listen carefully to the instructions? When you're asked to answer "Yes" or "No", please just answer "Yes" or "No", Mr. Kajmovic. I know it's difficult. Just give the name or other identity. From whom did you learn this information?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I cannot remember now, but I did receive such information.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was it from one person or more than one person?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: More than one, several persons, though I didn't see it and I cannot assert it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was it on the day itself or on a subsequent day or days, and if subsequently, how long after?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Roughly, I think it was a month and a half to two months when, on a couple of occasions, I left Stari Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No further. Paragraph 14, please. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice, go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I thought Judge Robinson wanted to -- no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 14 is the paragraph I said that we would return to last week, if necessary. I've reviewed the cross-examination, and I think it would probably be helpful to touch on it lightly. I want to take you back in time, Mr. Kajmovic, to the spring of 1992 and to the Bratstvo factory. You told us you were able to deal with an incident there. Were you present yourself at the Bratstvo factory at the incident in the spring of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you see the defendant Dario Kordic there?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How was he dressed?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: In HVO uniform, a camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: By whom or was he accompanied?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: In front of the factory, there were about 100 HVO soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What did Kordic do or say in your presence that concerned the factory and its contents?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: In view of the fact that the problem could not be resolved inside the factory, a meeting was scheduled in the municipality building of Novi Travnik. A meeting was held with representatives of the Bosniak and Croatian side, both military and civilian, and he insisted that he be given two multiple rocket launchers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was anything said about payment for the rocket launchers?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. At the meeting itself, the director of Bratstvo, I think his name was Krizanovic, said that this could not be taken just like that and that somebody had to pay for them. Then he said, "I would sign and the executive board of the municipal assembly of Busovaca would pay for those multiple rocket launchers."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: For clarity, who said he would sign?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Kordic said that he would sign. I think that he actually signed a piece of paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. I turn now briefly to one exhibit. To put to the end the matter that I know is subject of objection, can I put in a collection of photographs of Vitez? We can deal with them very briefly, but they will then be available for other evidence where photographs are helpful, if that happens. So can this Exhibit 2207 be provided to the Court and to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Kajmovic, have you seen this album of photographs yourself before?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: These are photographs of the Rijeka community centre in Vitez or, more specifically, the Rijeka neighbourhood community which was an HVO camp for a few days.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm going to go through them very quickly, and I just want you to confirm that the index is accurate in case we use the photographs on future occasions, bearing in mind, as I was informed by the interpreters last week, that when I did it too quickly in relation to another document, I made a mistake. So if we just turn over quickly, 2 is the Vitez police station; yes?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 3, the post office?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Post office in Vitez, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 4, the police station?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: That is the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 5, the public accounts office?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, known as the SDK in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. 6, the post office?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The post office in Vitez, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 7, a department store?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, the department store in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 8, 9 and 10, Hotel Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, the Hotel Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you know whose headquarters were contained there?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Blaskic's headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 11 and 12, the Workers' University?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 13, part of Hotel Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 14, the elementary school?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 15 through to 19, the Workers' University?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, yes, the Workers' University.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 20, Hotel Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Yes, this is the Hotel Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 21, the music school?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 22, Hotel Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 23, the municipality house, but I think you would say that these signs were put up after the conflict?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, the entrance to the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And you say the signs here were put up after --

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, after.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 24, the entrance to the municipality house?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, the entrance to the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 25, music school, police station?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. No, no. This photograph is the municipality building of Vitez, and to the left, you can see a little bit of the music school.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. 26, the music school?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The music school, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And 27?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, the same building.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 28, the hotel again; 29 --

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- the municipality building again, and 30, the hotel?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We then come to the next topic. Very briefly, you told us that you conducted for your thesis a population study; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As part of that study, did you research available material on the census of Vitez both before and after the conflict?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. I carried out research, and I came to certain conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you plot the information from available census material both on maps and in charts?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I understand there's an objection to the product of this work being laid before you, so I'll let the objection be made.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: With respect to the photographs, Your Honour, there is no objection. I had previously informed Mr. Nice that we objected to the proffer that's contained in paragraph 31 of this document, the outline of Mr. Kajmovic's testimony. The objection is a very simple one: Essentially, the Prosecutor is seeking to elicit from this witness expert testimony. In Blaskic, there was no requirement, I believe, in the Rules of Procedure, as they existed at that time, for the provision of expert witnesses' reports. Mr. Kajmovic was actually identified as and permitted to testify as an expert in the Blaskic case, an expert demographer and statistician and so forth, over the objection of the Defence. I believe that that was in the days before Rule 94 bis. Rule 94 bis states that any expert witness report has got to be provided to the Defence as soon as possible, but it shall be filed with the Trial Chamber not less than 21 days before the date on which the expert is expected to testify. Then another Rule comes into effect that puts the onus on the Defence to notify the Trial Chamber, within 14 days of the filing of such a report, whether it accepts the expert testimony or whether it intends to cross-examine the witness. This gentleman is actually not qualified as an expert witness. He is not impartial, for all of the reasons that he has previously testified about. He was the head of the SDA party in Vitez. But more importantly, and significantly insofar as the Blaskic case is concerned, this gentleman testified on January the 19th, 1998, I believe, he informed the Trial Chamber that a copy of his thesis was available if the Trial Chamber wished to see it, but he had yet to defend his thesis. Indeed, he told the Trial Chamber that he expected to defend the thesis in June of 1998. I think he said: "It will be presented this June in front of the faculty at the University of Sarajevo." In paragraph 3 of the proffer presented by the Prosecutor, the last sentence states that this thesis has yet to be defended before the faculty. I think that the Court should know that it is a master's thesis, a master's degree, not a doctor's thesis or anything like that. This gentleman is a history teacher from a small town; he has previously described Vitez as a fairly small municipality. He's not a statistician by training or by avocation; he's not an ethnographic expert, if such a thing even exists; he's not a demographer; and he still has yet to defend this master's thesis before the school of political science at the school of political science at the University of Sarajevo. We think that this report is going to be, (a), an expert report from someone who has not been identified in accordance with the mandatory requirements of Rule 94 bis; and (b), as he did in Blaskic, a mere conduit for many, many levels of hearsay evidence masquerading under the guise of a supposedly "expert" opinion. Furthermore, Mr. Kajmovic didn't employ any scientific methods. Instead, what he did was he went through the records that he got from the police station in Vitez, and he conducted, according to his Blaskic testimony, about 40 to 50 random interviews and admitted quite candidly to the Trial Chamber, to Judge Jorda, that he had not interviewed a single Croat. Indeed, Mr. Harmon, who was the sponsor of the expert opinion in that case, stated on page 5711 of the transcript that Mr. Kajmovic has explained why he could not do such research. That led to Judge Jorda being very troubled by the admission of this testimony, which he actually allowed in, in the days before Rule 94 bis, and I'd just like to quote Judge Jorda's observation, if I may, from the Bench in that trial, page 5740 of the Blaskic trial transcript. He said that "Because you have a thesis which corresponds to what you believe, and to your commitments in the SDA, and as a Judge, I'm somewhat disturbed that you have this thesis." And we are, too, Your Honours. We believe, in conclusion, that this is procedurally improper; it's a violation of the express, simple, easily understandable, and easily observable requirements of Rule 94 bis; and it jeopardises the right of the Defence to reasonable disclosure. We have never even seen the thesis. We have never been told what this gentleman is going to say. And he is not an expert; he is just a student, at present, who has got a thesis. For those reasons, we object to any attempt to introduce expert testimony through this percipient fact witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If the witness is not an expert, as this witness has not been categorised in this trial, but he is a witness who -- as a student, as you put it -- has made a study, why should that study not be admitted, whatever the niceties of whether the thesis has been defended or not? Why should he not be entitled to give evidence of the study and then the Court give it what weight it thinks it should have? You can cross-examine as to it. I'm not sure how significant the evidence is, but it will be open to you to do that. What is the damage and prejudice if that course is followed?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Because, Judge May, we have to cross-examine on the fly. We've never even seen the study or the report or any of the opinions. We have no idea what he is going to say, even, in his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What have you been given?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The only thing that we have, Your Honours, is a copy of the transcript of this gentleman's testimony in Blaskic, where he articulated a number of opinions; but even then, we couldn't tell what the basis for those opinions was, and nor could the Defence, because they hadn't been given the study either. So the way that the evidence came in was purely oral testimony, in a completely ad hoc way, and that's what we're confronted with right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, let me make some inquiries about this. Mr. Nice, I hadn't appreciated that there were no underlying documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There are four underlying documents. I'm sorry they hadn't been produced earlier; it's my oversight for not distributing them last week, I think, really. What it amounts to is that at paragraph 31, over the page, is the only conclusion I'm concerned to elicit from this witness, which are two rather modest conclusions. They're two statistical conclusions. They're not dissimilar from the sort of conclusions that people have been giving, by way of estimate, regularly throughout this trial when they're asked, "Well, by what percentage, in your estimate, did the population increase or decrease as to its ethnic composition, and so on, by what percentages did it change?" In the case of this witness, by reference to a couple of maps on which he's charted information and a couple of charts on which he has charted information, he can give the modest statistical conclusions that are contained in paragraph 31, and that's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: To the effect that part of the Muslim population left?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And that the Croat population increased?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's it. It may well be, in fact, that these aren't contested by the Defence as conclusions; I don't know. (Trial Chamber confers)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. President, allow me to add a couple of words which may help to clarify the matter. First of all, I should like to confirm that we never received these documents, and therefore I'm convinced that we cannot conduct the cross-examination properly, because we have no way of verifying those data within a couple of hours or during the day. It seems to me that that would be highly prejudicial for the Defence, if it has no time to verify the data, on the basis of the Rules that my learned friend has already referred to. As for the substance of data that we might learn from this, I should like to recall that in the supporting material, the Prosecution has offered official statistical data; that is, the population census of the official institution responsible for this. That was the Statistical Institute of the former Yugoslavia and the Statistical Institute of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. So that was the basic data; that is the ethnic structure of the population before the outbreak of conflicts, because it was mere chance that census was carried out in 1991, and we received those materials as part of the supporting material. As for the migrations that occurred in the course of the conflict, I assure you there is a host of official data produced by various institutions, among which, I can tell you from memory, there are the parish authorities of the new Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina; then there are the data of the federal authorities of the Federation, on which the financing and reconstruction of returnees' homes is being financed. These are exhaustive data. Some of them I have seen myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. Kovacic, I think we all wish to avoid wasting too much time. In reality, one testimony does not exclude others. If there is an evaluation to be given, it is up to the Chamber to judge the weight of it. This does not mean to say that there is no other information coming from other sources and which will also be conveyed to the Chamber, either by the Prosecution or the Defence. Therefore I think we should try to save time, hearing one estimate that is not a global expertise, or thesis. Regardless of the level of that thesis, it is simply a question put by the Prosecution to the witness. Do you have a fundamental objection if this witness is asked for his estimate, for what it's worth? I think these are not crucial issues, and we should avoid too much argument over them. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Your Honours, in answer to the question you have put to me, the answer is yes, I do have an objection, because I think that such a matter will be part of the record as an opinion of an expert person whom we are indirectly proclaiming to be an expert witness. As for saving time, my objection is partly along those lines too. Instead of focusing on qualitative, trustworthy evidence, which it is up to the Prosecution to provide, we are substituting existing and accessible data with non-reliable sources, and we are wasting time in the process. That is my point. Thank you. (Trial Chamber confers)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We really are concerned about the time being wasted in this trial on what is a relatively trivial issue. First of all, this witness is not being put forward as an expert. Now, it may be that in some jurisdictions, people other than experts cannot give their opinion. That rule does not apply, as far as I know, in this jurisdiction. This witness has made a study of the topic, and in our judgement he's perfectly entitled to put forward what his conclusions are. The issue is a relatively narrow one and not, I should have thought, of great significance. If the Defence wish to cross-examine at length on it, they will be subject to the direction of the Court, but no doubt any relevant documents can be disclosed. Meanwhile, other evidence, no doubt, can be called about it, if there are better sources, by the Defence. But we really hope not too much time is going to be taken up with what looks to be a very small point. Yes. Call the evidence, and briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can the witness, I think, have collectively the table 2140, table 2153? That's in B/C/S, but it's probably -- and it's got the English and French translations attached to it. Can he also have the map 2141 and the map 2154? Please put the demographic map for 1991 on the ELMO. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you prepare this document as part of your studies; "Yes" or "No"?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The dots are keyed as to the ethnic origin of people resident in particular areas; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: From where did you get the information that identifies those who were Croats, Bosniaks, Serbs and then Yugoslavians and others? Where did you get the information from?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It was like this: If I may just briefly comment, the objection of the Defence --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I don't want you to comment, I want you to -- no, don't bother with what happens in Court. Please listen to the questions. Just tell us, where did you get the information as translated in blue, red, green, and black dots?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, these are official statistical data, rather the data of the statistical administration of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, dating to 1991, so these are official data.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Can he have the demographic map for 1996, which is another map that looks like this? I trust the Court has got it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Would you mind putting it on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This relates to 1996 and to a smaller area. From where did you get this information?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, these are the results I arrived at through the investigation and analysis of different sources. The ethnic composition of the population in the municipality of Vitez looks more or less as it is represented on this map. New figures will become available only after a new census. Of course, there hasn't been a census now but there are some estimates of the statistical administration of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and they are at very little variance with the figures that I arrived at. I even think that the figures that I came to are more accurate than the estimates of the statistical administration of the Republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's all I wanted. May we look, please, then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. Nice, the Court does need to know certain things. There is a legend here explaining different colours, and we need a minimum interpretation, if possible. Could I have the translation of the legend of these symbols, the thing that is in a box here? We cannot read Serbo-Croatian, and I can't see any other language that I would understand, explaining what the signs mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Kajmovic, will you look at the box? Perhaps the unit could focus down on the box and enlarge it on the ELMO. The box contains a key. Can you tell us, the first colour in blue, "Hrvati" is "Croat", the second in green is Bosniak?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The third, "Ostali" is "Other"?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The black line means what?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The black line means the boundaries of the Vitez municipality, between the Vitez municipality and other municipalities, but there is an error here. The dotted line is the boundary between the Vitez and adjacent municipalities, and the full line is practically the line separating the part of the Vitez municipality which continued under the HVO control and the other part which remained under the administrative control of the lawful BH authorities. These green, blue and white circles indicate the ethnic structure or, rather, the exchange after the aggression. Of course, we have here the data showing that the Croat population in the municipality of Vitez has risen by some 20 per cent, that it was about 45 per cent formerly and it has reached some 64,98, and correspondingly, of course, a drop in the share of the Bosniak population expelled from the territory of the Vitez municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The drop in the Bosniak population was by what percentage, approximately?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The drop was -- well, we have it here. From 41 to 33,763 per cent, so it would make a decline of about seven per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's all I need, save only for this: There are two tables produced to the Court which you might just look at to identify, numbers 2140 and 2153. Do those tables contain -- and here the documents are in B/C/S, English and French. Do those documents contain, in tabulated form, information about population at various locations including Vitez? Just "Yes" or "No" to that.

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. You can answer questions about that, if asked. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, this table shows the ethnic structure according to the 1991 census. According to the so-called --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Kajmovic, you've given the evidence we need, the table is self-explanatory, and it may be the others will ask you questions. Maybe they won't. Thank you. You'll be asked further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Who is going to cross-examine?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. President, I should first like to suggest that we be given some time to prepare for the cross-examination. I am suggesting this because this witness, less perhaps so on Friday, but today very evidently was examined in much greater detail and much greater depth than indicated by his previous statements. We were quite taken by surprise by some things that today we could not find all that detail in earlier statements, not even in the Prosecutor's summary could we find anything, or there were discrepancies between the statements in summaries and the evidence of the witness, and for no other reason than for a more rational approach to cross-examination and to avoid repetition and going back to some of the subjects. Secondly, in view of the breadth and the surprises, we should also like to ask for your permission to split it. We have two Defence counsel in this matter, and we should like to split it in two, for one to examine the witness as to his evidence and the other one to go through the diary which was given us under the discovery period, so that we could proceed quicker. We should like to start our cross-examination tomorrow, because there were a number of new facts which we did not hear before and we did not hear from our client either. Thank you. (Trial Chamber confers)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Sayers, are you ready to cross-examine?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Kovacic, we're not going to allow two cross-examinations. Only one is allowed. It's more than enough per accused. Secondly, you've got until half past 2.00 to get ready. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. Kajmovic, my name is Steve Sayers. I represent Dario Kordic. Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I believe, sir, that you have given two previous statements to the investigators helping the Prosecutor in this case. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: One, as far as I know, in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You gave a statement to Mr. Gerns on July 13, 1995; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: A lady by the name of Emina Kaknjo was present at that interview, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't remember what was the interpreter's name.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Well, according to the face page of your statement, sir, John Gerns was the interviewer. You remember him?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I believe it was a Pakistani.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The interpreter, and forgive me for my abysmal pronunciation, is Adisa Karamuratovic. Do you remember her?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I don't. There were several interpreters and I don't remember all these things, because the statement was made one day and then the next day there were corrections made to it and then checks. There were further conversations related to the statement. I really can't go into the method used by the investigation team.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
